articles.title: Why has the Yemen government called for a general mobilisation?
articles.summary: Yemeni government offers amnesty to Houthi defectors, aiming to weaken rebel ranks and rebuild national unity.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has called for a general mobilisation of the population as part of its long-anticipated pushback against the Houthis.

In his first speech since government forces were routed from the Red Sea coast, Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, made a national call to arms and asked citizens to “contribute in every way possible” in the fight against the Houthis.

Al-Alimi also offered an amnesty to defecting Houthi fighters, effective immediately.

It comes as the Houthis made dramatic advances in western Yemen in September, including capturing the city of Mocha and Mayyun Island. The assault follows the recent collapse of a 2022 government and Houthi truce, which had paused 12 years of fighting between the two sides.

The Houthis’ Red Sea offensive has given them control over Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the busiest shipping routes in the world, a narrow waterway linking the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

The strait is also of crucial economic and strategic importance to Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government.

Through the mobilisation of the general population, al-Alimi pledged to recapture Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, which it lost to the Houthis in 2014, and restore government sovereignty over the whole of Yemen.

“Our objective is clear to everyone both at home and abroad: to restore state institutions and exercise their sovereignty over the entire country, including Sanaa,” al-Alimi said.

So, why has the government decided to call for a general mobilisation now and why has the government offered Houthi fighters an amnesty? Here’s what we know.

Why has al-Alimi ordered a general mobilisation?

In the eyes of most analysts, the government’s position has rarely been weaker. Pushed out of Mocha, Mayyun Island and the wider Bab al-Mandeb coastline, the Houthi advance jeopardises the authority of the internationally recognised government and brings its Saudi ally deeper into the conflict. Riyadh and other Saudi cities have now become regular targets of Houthi rockets and drones.

Even the government’s rare victories have proven short-lived. Hays district in al-Hodeidah was briefly taken by government forces in early September before falling again to the Houthis just days later.

Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera Arabic’s Yemen affairs editor, described al-Alimi’s comments as a “war speech”, calling for Yemenis to join the military’s ranks and take part in the liberation of Houthi-held Sanaa.

Government forces currently remain bogged down in fighting in Taiz and Marib, far from the capital.

How significant is the offer of amnesty?

In 2024, before the current lightning advance, a United Nations panel of experts estimated that Houthi fighters numbered somewhere around 350,000, bolstered by the recruitment of fighters sometimes aged under 18.

It is unlikely that these fighters will defect to the government side any time soon, analysts have said, but the offer of amnesty might grow more attractive if the Houthis begin to lose ground.

“You need to remember that, despite everything, Yemen remains a tribal society,” Baraa Shiban, a researcher and political analyst on Yemen and the Gulf at the Royal United Service Institute (RUSI), said. “The offer of amnesty is the government signalling that it won’t be seeking revenge upon fighters in a way that could risk the conflict descending into tribal warfare.”

Saudi Arabia has a lot to lose. In the last 24 hours, Riyadh claimed to have intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles targeting the Yanbu area on the Red Sea and Taif, to the country’s West.

The potential for further strikes upon Saudi Arabia threatens Riyadh’s ability to export oil through the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia’s west coast has gained greater significance since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28, with Tehran responding by closing the Strait of Hormuz, blocking access by sea to the kingdom’s oil-rich Eastern Province.

The brief closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West Crude Oil Pipeline following an attack on three pumping stations earlier this month has also exposed vulnerabilities for Riyadh.

On Thursday, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan – who signed their Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August – announced that an emergency meeting of military chiefs would be held to address the threat.

However, what level of intervention the three countries might take in Yemen, if any, remained far from certain.

“Even at the peak of the fighting [before the 2022 ceasefire], Saudi only deployed very limited ground forces in support of the government, preferring to rely on air strikes instead,” Shiban said.

“I really can’t imagine Yemeni citizens reacting all that well to the sight of armed Turkish, Pakistani and Saudi forces on their soil, which could even risk taking the conflict in a very different direction.

“I would be surprised if their [Turkiye and Pakistan] involvement did extend beyond technical support and intelligence sharing.”

The Houthis have said they would keep Bab al-Mandeb open and indicated that any attacks would be limited to Saudi vessels. However, addressing the United Nations General Assembly last week, the vice-president of Yemen’s internationally recognised government council, Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer, said the rebels were not to be trusted.

“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” he told world leaders in New York on Thursday.

Protecting the strait “is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation,” Alimi-Bawzer said.

Saudi Arabia has announced a naval coalition for the Red Sea, but details of the scale and scope of the armada remain largely unknown.

The Houthis, meanwhile, have reportedly sent a letter to the European Union promising that ships linked to the bloc would not be targeted, in an apparent attempt to isolate Saudi Arabia from its allies.

articles.title: This popular sound machine for babies was just recalled over fire and burn risk
articles.summary: Love to Dream recalled its portable baby sound machine over a battery fire and burn risk. Here’s how to check your model and date code and get a refund.
articles.body: If you use a Love to Dream sound machine to help your baby drift off, you’ll want to pay attention to this news: The brand has recalled their portable white noise machine because its lithium-ion battery can overheat while charging with an incompatible charger, posing a risk of fire and burns. Below, find everything you need to know about the recall, including how to check whether your sound machine is affected. Why was the Love to Dream sound machine recalled? Love to Dream recalled its Sleep Machine because the device’s lithium-ion battery can overheat while charging if it’s connected to a charger that isn’t compatible with the unit. That overheating poses a risk of injury from fire and burns, a serious concern for a product that’s often kept in a nursery. The recall applies only to the Love to Dream Sleep Machine with model number LTD-SM23 and date code 7W15TN. The recalled product is a white, heart-shaped portable white noise machine with a night light and a tan carry strap. You can find the date code printed on the side of the machine or on the back of its box, and Love to Dream says units with any other date code are not affected and aren’t part of the recall. The affected machines were sold from February 2025 through September 2026, and Love to Dream is conducting the recall in cooperation with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. The company’s recall notice doesn’t say how many units are affected or whether any overheating incidents or injuries have been reported. What to do if you have the recalled sound machine If your Love to Dream Sleep Machine has model number LTD-SM23 and date code 7W15TN, stop using it immediately. Disconnect it from any charger and put it somewhere safe, away from anything flammable or anything that could damage it. Then visit lovetodream.com/recall to find out how to dispose of the device and claim your refund. Because the machine contains a lithium-ion battery, you should not toss it in your household trash or recycling bin. Instead, dispose of it only according to your local requirements for lithium-ion products. If you have questions, you can contact Love to Dream by email at recall@lovetodream.com or by calling toll-free at 1-833-753-3710. Other portable sound machines to use instead The below portable sound machines have not been recalled and can be safely used. The Hatch Go is a rechargeable sound machine for babies on the go. It plays 10 soothing sounds, like white noise and heartbeat, and has three buttons plus a ring to clip onto a stroller or diaper bag. It needs no app, WiFi or Bluetooth, and lasts up to 15 hours per charge. The Yogasleep Hushh is a compact portable sound machine with three sounds: bright white noise, deep white noise and gentle surf. It weighs just 3.8 ounces, has an amber night light and child lock, and clips onto a stroller, car seat or crib. It runs up to 24 hours per charge. With 20 soothing sounds and an amber night light you can dim, this portable machine from Momcozy works for nursery and travel alike. It clips onto a stroller, crib or diaper bag, and includes a timer, child lock and auto shut-off. It charges via USB-C and is designed to last all night. Why trust NBC Selected? I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness and lifestyle, among other topics. I have also written about the cyclosporiasis outbreak, the recent recall on eggs and how to relieve shoulder pain. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: VAN HIPP: Why the Army should restore its grassroots link to America's communities
articles.summary: The Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army program was terminated in June 2025, severing a century-old link between the U.S. Army and Main Street.
articles.body: I first wrote about the "Forgotten Americans" in early 2016 in an opinion piece for Fox News. The phrase was actually coined by Pat Buchanan when he served as a presidential speechwriter for President Nixon. Nixon used it in at least one speech, but then started using the phrase "Silent Majority." In my piece, I talked about who the "Forgotten Americans" really are. They love their families and want a better life for their kids. They believe in American exceptionalism. They work hard, worship their God, and go to church. They pay their taxes and obey the law. When America's security is threatened, the Forgotten Americans are always the first to volunteer to defend it. They want to see America's border secured, and they're concerned about "political correctness" being taught to their children in schools that they fund. A few months after my op-ed, the Trump campaign started using the phrase "Forgotten Americans," and it was a central part of President Trump's acceptance speech at the 2016 Republican National Convention. RENEWED PATRIOTISM AND CAREER OPPORTUNITIES FUEL ARMY'S BIGGEST RECRUITING SURGE IN YEARS For over 100 years, there's been no better link between the U.S. military and grassroots Americans than the Army's Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army (CASA) Program. Historically, the Secretary of the Army has appointed at least one individual in each state to serve as a Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army. That person has usually been a business or civic leader who serves in a purely voluntary capacity, but has served as the link for telling the "Army story" and building support for the U.S. military in local communities. In fact, on the U.S. Army’s own website, it’s referred to as "The Army’s Link to the People." I believe we can have a laser focus on the technology America needs to protect our national security interests and keep the American people safe while still engaging with the grassroots and telling the Army story at the local level. Over the years, the CASAs have gone into schools in rural America to tell the Army story and instill patriotism among our nation's youth. They've also been a big asset in working with Army recruiters to address recruiting challenges at the local level. Fortunately, today, we have a secretary of War who has gotten personally involved to help ensure we meet our active-duty recruiting goals, but that hasn’t always been the case. Meeting a recruiting goal does not end the need to earn the trust of the next generation of soldiers and families. MCCHRYSTAL, BRIDGELAND: WANT TO STRENGTHEN AMERICA? REQUIRE A YEAR OF NATIONAL SERVICE CASAs have also offered tremendous support for our "Soldier for Life" program. The Soldier for Life program supports our soldiers as they transition out of uniform and into civilian life. CASAs have connected transitioning soldiers with local employers and guided them through other decisions they must make during the transition to civilian life. Over the years, I've been impressed, too, with the volunteer work of CASAs in helping military families facing a particular need. Unfortunately, in June 2025, the decision was made to terminate the entire Corps of Civilian Aides to the Secretary of the Army. In making the move, Army leadership said they wanted to focus more on technology than community engagement. I certainly understand the role of technology on today's modern battlefield. In fact, I had the honor last year of giving one of the keynote addresses at Taiwan's annual National Security Summit. In my remarks, I specifically focused on artificial intelligence, quantum, and spectrum as the equalizers of the battlefield of the future. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION I believe we can have a laser focus on the technology America needs to protect our national security interests and keep the American people safe while still engaging with the grassroots and telling the Army story at the local level. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Army needs the innovation of Silicon Valley. It also needs the commitment of Main Street and the regular people who answer the call to serve — our Forgotten Americans. It’s time to restore the CASA program’s traditional, community-based role. Building the Army of the future should not mean losing its link to the people. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM VAN HIPP

articles.title: Turkiye calls for UN Security Council veto to end: Could it happen?
articles.summary: Fully abolishing the veto would require the unlikely agreement of all five permanent Security Council members.
articles.body:
Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has called for the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) to lose their veto power, arguing that the current veto system is “unjust” and hinders “global stability and peace”.

The call comes as the UNSC, which has five permanent members and 10 rotating, non-permanent members, remains deadlocked on many issues – from Israel’s war on Gaza to Russia’s war in Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz.

The US, one of the five permanent members, has vetoed seven resolutions related to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict over the past three years, including five calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.

Russian vetoes have prevented the UNSC from passing any firm resolutions on the war in Ukraine.

Speaking to journalists in New York on Thursday, Erdogan said, “Let the veto mechanism be abolished… Let us move from a UN model that protects only five members to a mechanism that encompasses all members”.

So, could Erdogan’s call become a reality and what would abolishing the veto mean for the UNSC?

What is the UNSC veto and who can exercise it?

It is a special power to veto any substantive resolution, granted to the body’s five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China.

It means that even if 14 of 15 UNSC members vote in favour of a resolution, just one veto from any of the five permanent members (P5) can tank it.

Erdogan has called for a complete overhaul of the UNSC. That includes ending permanent membership of the council and eliminating the veto power.

Laying out his case in a September 22 article published by Bloomberg, Erdogan wrote that the UNSC’s current structure, developed eight decades ago, no longer meets the needs of a changing world and that a single country should not be able to block the wishes of the broader international community.

“Leaving the resolution of global crises to the will of a handful of capitals is no longer compatible with the realities of today’s world,” he wrote.

Erdogan also called for greater powers for the UN General Assembly (UNGA), which he said should elect all UNSC members for set terms. Countries seeking to serve on the council would therefore have to “regain the confidence of the majority of member states through elections”, he said.

Erdogan lobbied for this initiative during his recent address to the UNGA , saying “a system in which the will of more than 190 countries is subject to the whims of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust”.

What would it take for the UNSC to decide to end the veto?

Formally ending the veto would require an amendment to the UN Charter.

Under Article 108, that requires approval by two-thirds of the UNGA and ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent members. In other words, the P5 would have to sign off on giving up their own veto power.

What is the France-Mexico proposal that is gaining ground?

In 2015, France and Mexico tabled a proposal urging the P5 to suspend their vetoes on resolutions involving mass atrocities, such as genocide and crimes against humanity.

The initiative would rely on a “collective and voluntary agreement” among P5 states.

The initiative has recently gained renewed traction, with 21 states, including P5 member the UK, backing it within the last four months.

That brings the total number of UN members states supporting it to 128, according to the French government, just one short of the number needed to pass a resolution in the UNGA.

While such a resolution would be non-binding, advocates hope it would exert more pressure on P5 states to withhold their votes in emergency situations.

Any formal effort to abolish P5 members’ veto power is likely to fail, as it would inevitably face resistance from most, if not all, P5 members.

Russia has already responded to the Turkish initiative by saying it believes permanent UNSC members should retain their veto power, though it did say it supports expanding the number of permanent members on the council.

The US and China have previously strongly defended their veto privileges.

Expanding the UNSC, as Russia proposed, is more likely, though that would also come with challenges.

The US and China have both previously said they would support modest increases to the council’s composition, including by adding seats for African nations, none of which hold permanent membership. The UK and France have also backed expansion, including permanent seats for Brazil, Germany, India and Japan, as well as African countries.

But expanding the UNSC would also require an amendment to the UN Charter, which again requires the backing of all P5 states. Getting the P5 to agree on which countries to share their power with – and whether to extend new members the veto power – has long proved difficult .

“The status quo is not really interested in change,” Professor Ibrahim Gambari, a former Nigerian foreign minister and former Nigerian permanent representative to the UN, told Al Jazeera.

As for the France-Mexico initiative, analysts say its impact would be limited because the commitments are voluntary and non-binding.

Writing in a 2022 article for US publication Lawfare, analysts John Ramming Chappell and Emma Svoboda noted that the France-Mexico initiative and others like it are “couched in voluntary language” and lack consensus “from the most frequent veto-users (Russia, the United States and China)”.

As a result, “the principles advanced in the initiatives remain aspirational”, they wrote.

Who has exercised the veto most in the past?

Historically, Russia (or the Soviet Union prior to 1991) has cast the most vetoes by far, with nearly half of all vetoes ever recorded (163 out of 331).

The US is second, with 95 vetoes – around 28 percent of those cast.

In recent years, the US has vetoed numerous resolutions concerning the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including five calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it has vetoed three resolutions relating to that conflict.

When have France and the UK exercised the veto?

France and the UK – the two permanent members calling for suspension of the veto in resolutions relating to humanitarian atrocities – have exercised their veto far more sparingly, with a combined 50 vetoes. Neither country has used a veto since 1989 and most of their earlier vetoes were cast alongside the US.

The UK has only been the sole veto on a resolution a handful of times, all related to its former colony Rhodesia, which later became independent as Zimbabwe.

France has only vetoed a resolution on its own twice, once in connection with a territorial dispute with Comoros and the other related to the Indonesian conflict in 1947.

articles.title: The intelligence war is turning against the Houthis
articles.summary: Russian-Iranian intelligence helped the Houthis’ offensive on the Red Sea coast. Now that system is under attack.
articles.body:
The collapse of Yemen’s western front was not primarily the result of sheer Houthi numbers. It resulted from a fused Russian-Iranian command system in which elements of Russia’s space-based geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) and signals intelligence (SIGINT) capabilities were integrated into an Iranian-led command-and-control (C2) system supporting Houthi operations. Human penetration of Tariq Saleh’s National Resistance Forces gave that system the access required to turn technical collection into a battlefield advantage.

Through Project AURORAH, the GEOINT and SIGINT fusion system I created, I identified and sequenced Russian military reconnaissance over Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, the UAE and Jordan during the Iran-US war. A compartmented special-access programme (SAP) within the project reconstructed Russian orbital collection as a single multisensor system, including the sequences that preceded Iran’s precision strikes on countries across the region and on US military assets. That work later considerably assisted a major CNN investigation into Russian military geospatial satellite support for Iranian precision targeting across the Middle East.

The underlying principle had already emerged over Iran: orbital intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) was no longer merely supporting operations, but helping construct the operational picture of the battlespace before strikes were carried out. That use of satellite intelligence was already visible during the Iran war . Russian GEOINT mapped how forces were deployed, their movement corridors, headquarters and logistical changes, while SIGINT mapped the sources of electronic signals, communications patterns and command relationships.

The advantage came from sequencing different forms of satellite collection over time, not from any single spacecraft. Different reconnaissance satellites provided complementary geographic and electromagnetic coverage, allowing changes in how forces moved and operated to be followed over time rather than captured as isolated snapshots. During the Iran war, this combination of different forms of satellite intelligence had already shown how Russian satellite intelligence could sharpen Iranian precision operations.

In Yemen, Iran provided the operational integration. Russian-derived intelligence was combined with Houthi tactical reporting and human access to build a detailed picture of how Tariq Saleh’s command actually functioned: which headquarters remained responsive, where reported positions diverged from reality, which formations were poorly coordinated, and where gaps existed in command, reporting and communications between the National Resistance Forces (NRF) and the Saudi-led Joint Forces Command (JFC). That picture made weaknesses along the western coastal front possible to exploit.

This is where the front broke. One command-and-control pathway connected JFC headquarters with elements of the NRF; another connected those forces with one another and with their own senior command. Once both became unreliable, inaccurate information flowed upwards while confused or manipulated instructions flowed downwards.

The consequences were specific. One NRF commander acknowledged an order to hold a blocking position and then withdrew. Another reported that a non-NRF Yemeni formation had vacated a military airfield when personnel were still there, giving commanders an inaccurate picture of where friendly forces were positioned and contributing to casualties after a strike. A Saudi special forces task force at Mokha was the first to recognise that reported force deployments no longer matched the reality on the ground.

Saudi strike missions had been prepared, but airpower could not be used freely when the locations of friendly forces could no longer be reliably confirmed. The problem was compounded when some NRF brigades discovered during activation that 50 to 60 percent of registered personnel had failed to report, despite months of JFC biometric registration, salary restoration and force consolidation. As coordination around the critical military hub of Jabal al-Nar deteriorated, NRF formations began leaving positions before the main Houthi forces had reached them.

That debacle has become the central learning event of the campaign. Combined Saudi-Yemeni and Saudi-Pakistani Joint Terminal Attack Controller (JTAC) teams are now being embedded with major northern formations, restoring an authenticated link between forces on the ground and the JFC’s strike system. Saudi Operational Mentoring and Liaison Teams (OMLT) are also providing direct links to the JFC and independently verifying the manpower, location and readiness of Yemeni formations. At the same time, positive authentication of commands, compartmented reporting and redundant encrypted communications are closing the vulnerabilities exposed at Mokha.

Saudi Arabia has used a similar approach before, against a different adversary. In January 2026, JFC military counterintelligence mapped and systematically degraded the Abu Dhabi command-and-control system supporting Southern Transitional Council (STC) operations in southern Yemen, while liaison and targeting mechanisms maintained a reliable picture of operations on the ground. Once that external layer was removed, UAE task forces and aligned formations rapidly lost their freedom of action and withdrew under pressure from the Saudi-led campaign.

The system now supporting the Houthis is far more sophisticated. Russia provides satellite-based intelligence and signals intelligence; Iran integrates that information into Houthi command and operations. But that sophistication also creates vulnerabilities: the system depends on secure communications, specialist personnel, intelligence-fusion nodes, technical advisers and continuous links between Sanaa and battlefield headquarters.

Those vulnerabilities are now being targeted. On the evening of September 19, the Iranian-led top-level command-and-control structure in Sanaa suffered a massive blow. Confirmed senior Houthi battlefield losses now include at least two major generals, seven brigadier generals and 32 colonels, many removed alongside their immediate aides, staff and communications elements. There are also strong indications that figures above the rank of major general have been neutralised within the highest levels of the Houthi command structure, together with associated foreign personnel, although those details remain deliberately withheld for now.

The effect is more important than the count. Front-line command is being systematically degraded while senior command nodes in Sanaa are simultaneously coming under precise JFC air strikes, disrupting the chain between intelligence collection, decision-making, targeting and execution. Headquarters forced to relocate, surviving commanders attempting to reconnect with subordinate units and remaining junior Iranian advisers establishing alternative pathways all generate fresh signatures that can be detected, correlated and geolocated.

This is why the Houthi advance is now struggling to reproduce the momentum of the West Coast breakthrough. The command links they exploited are being hardened, while their own externally supported command-and-control network is being progressively blinded and exposed. The failure on the West Coast has therefore become a lesson the Saudi-led forces are acting on, rather than a permanent weakness in their military structure.

The Saudi-led JFC’s broader transformation in C6ISR – the systems connecting command, communications, intelligence and combat capabilities – target development and faster sensor-to-shooter integration has changed the military equation since 2015. At the same time, sustained Houthi escalation has exhausted the restraint that governed Saudi policy for years . The major Saudi-led campaign now taking shape will therefore begin against an adversary whose external command support is already under sustained attack.

That is the decisive difference. The Russian-Iranian system sustaining and amplifying Houthi military power is being degraded before major Saudi-led air, land and naval operations are fully under way, while the tactical failures exposed at Mokha are being corrected within the Saudi-led JFC. The Houthis exploited a compromised command system once; they are now being forced to fight while the external system that magnified their own effectiveness is systematically dismantled.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: South Gloucestershire WW2 veteran Harry Francis dies aged 101
articles.summary: The decorated veteran of the Royal Marines and SBS carried out missions behind enemy lines.
articles.body:
One of the West of England's last surviving veterans from World War Two has passed away aged 101.

Harry Francis, from South Gloucestershire, joined the Royal Navy in 1942 at 16, having lied about his age to serve.

He went on to join the Royal Marines and became one of the first men to join the Special Boat Service (SBS), carrying out covert operations in Italy, Lebanon and Burma, where he was wounded.

South Gloucestershire Armed Forces Day put out a tribute on social media where organisers said: "His quiet bravery and his remarkable life will not be forgotten."

"Harry belonged to a generation that gave everything so that we could live in freedom. His quiet bravery, and his remarkable life, will not be forgotten," they said.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Gwen, his children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and all who knew and loved H."

The organisation went on to say how Francis celebrated his centenary last year surrounded by family and friends.

He was also visited by the Royal Marines Reserve Bristol, whose personnel delivered a personal message from the First Sea Lord and Chief of the Naval Staff General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, recognising him for his extraordinary courage.

His daughter Teresa Betton previously told the BBC: "What he gave for this country, all the friends that he lost... I'm so proud of him.

"He tells the stories, but not all of them. He signed the [Official] Secrets Act and has stuck by it."

In a tribute on Facebook, Charlie Liston said, when she was younger, they were neighbours and remembered how Francis had helped her with a school project about the war.

"Sat in his dining room with a cup of tea Gwen had made, Harry told me just a small portion of his many many experiences whilst fighting in Burma," Liston said.

"These stories made me very moved, both with tears and laughter.

"Harry was a very special person, not just as a public figure, but as a mentor, a neighbour, as a friend. He will be missed dearly."

articles.title: Roads flood in New Jersey, inundate some homes, as major signs of nor’easter take shape
articles.summary: More than 70,000 customers were without electricity in the U.S. Northeast on Saturday, the effect of a powerful nor’easter expected to create dangerous conditions through the weekend.
articles.body: Floodwaters covered streets in coastal New Jersey on Saturday morning as a powerful nor’easter battered the Northeast, knocking out electricity for more than 70,000 customers and threatening dangerous conditions through the weekend. Videos verified by NBC News showed heavy tidal flooding at Shelter Marina in Beach Haven. In nearby Beach Haven Crest, ducks swam along flooded streets. A resident’s video from Spray Beach showed water covering a fire hydrant and entering garages. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Saturday that she had declared a state of emergency the day before as the storm bore down on Long Island, New York City and Westchester County. The state expected 4 to 6 inches of rain on Long Island and 3 to 6 inches in New York City over three days, she said, but coastal flooding was its greatest concern. Tens of millions of people are in the path of the storm. The National Weather Service warned of dangerous flooding along the mid-Atlantic coast, particularly near New Jersey and Delaware, as well as winds strong enough to down trees and power lines. “This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend,” the weather service said Saturday. “Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses.” Hochul said about 22,000 customers in New York were without power and that swift-water recuse teams had been deployed in Nassau and Suffolk counties. State emergency management officials warned that high tides could bring more flooding Saturday night and Sunday morning, while rain could continue into Monday. In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water, with waves rippling along its surface, flooded the streets, inundating some homes. About 34 miles up the coast, in the borough of Manasquan, where some roads were also flooding, Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected “a lot of water in the streets for a long time.” A voluntary evacuation had been issued earlier in some low-lying areas of the community. Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard on Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some East Coast flights through the weekend. New Jersey communities prepare for major flooding Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds of up to 50 mph and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday. “It’s going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event,” Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. “I hope I’m wrong, but that’s my gut feeling.” Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees. Damaging winds threaten coastal New England Peak wind gusts could approach 60-65 mph on Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket in Massachusetts on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50-55 mph around Boston and 35-40 mph farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with the NWS in Norton, Massachusetts. “It’s definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you’re likely to see,” Belk said. Belk said nor’easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said. Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph, according to the NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could be almost as strong, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines. Storm disrupts concerts, baseball and flights Air travel was also being disrupted, with Boston particularly hard hit. Flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 39 cancellations at Boston Logan International Airport between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. Saturday, compared with 22 at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport. Another 12 flights were delayed at Logan. Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday-afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm. The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water. In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday. For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is “part of life,” said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled. “It’s a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point,” he said. “This is not out of the realm of ordinary.” Ashley Destino of Gloucester, a coastal city in northern Massachusetts, enjoyed a stroll along the beach with her two young children before preparing to hunker down at home during the storm. “We came to the beach on Friday afternoon because we knew we were going to be inside all weekend,” said Destino, who has Legos and arts and crafts activities prepared to entertain her two children, ages 7 and 4. She also prepared by securing her boat with additional lines, and her husband pulled out a generator in case the electricity goes out.

articles.title: A New York highway superintendent built a snow-fence pole remover from an old golf-cart wheel and scrap box tubing for $0; it cut a three-week job to about 1.5 weeks and has now won a national federal award
articles.summary: A discarded golf-cart wheel and a piece of scrap box tubing have earned a New York highway department national recognition.
articles.body: A discarded golf-cart wheel and a piece of scrap box tubing have earned a New York highway department national recognition. Riverhead Highway Superintendent Mike Zaleski built a simple snow-fence pole remover after seeing workers struggle to pull frozen poles from the ground by hand. The homemade tool cost nothing, reduced a job that once took about three weeks to roughly a week and a half, and helped prevent the back strain and injuries associated with the old method. The Riverhead News-Review reported that the invention won the Pioneer Award in the Federal Highway Administration’s 2026 Build a Better Mousetrap national competition. FHWA says the award recognised Riverhead’s use of entirely repurposed materials to reduce physical strain while improving productivity and safety. The invention is a reminder that meaningful public-works innovation can begin with scrap, observation and practical skill.A demanding winter routineEach year, the Riverhead Highway Department installs miles of snow fence to help control drifting snow.Snow fences are commonly placed near roads, open fields and other exposed areas where wind can carry snow onto the roadway. By slowing the wind, the fence encourages snow to settle before it reaches traffic lanes.The work is useful during winter, but it creates another demanding task when the season ends. Crews must remove the fencing and pull the supporting poles from the frozen ground.For years, workers handled that part manually. They gripped the poles, loosened them and pulled them out one by one. The process required repeated bending, lifting and force, often over many hours and across a large area.Riverhead Highway Superintendent Mike Zaleski saw the effect on his crew. Workers experienced back strain and other injuries, while the complete removal operation took about three weeks.“It’s strenuous, guys were getting hurt, it takes forever,” Zaleski told the Riverhead News-Review.An idea built from scrapZaleski decided that the department needed a tool that could pull poles from the ground without requiring workers to use their backs and arms for every lift.The resulting Snow Fence Pole Remover is made from an old golf-cart wheel and a piece of steel box tubing. The department built it using repurposed materials already available, so the cost was effectively zero.The tool consists of a single wheel attached to a steel frame. A section of box tubing slides over the snow-fence pole and grips it securely. The worker then uses the frame and wheel to create leverage and lift the pole from the ground.The mechanism is simple, but it changes the physics of the task. Rather than trying to pull a deeply embedded pole straight upward, the operator can use the wheel and frame to multiply force and guide the pole out.No motor, hydraulic pump or battery is required. The design relies on leverage, a stable frame and a wheel that allows the device to move easily from one pole to the next.Faster work and fewer injuriesThe most immediate benefit was the reduction in working time.Before the tool was introduced, the department needed approximately three weeks to remove the snow-fence poles. With the Snow Fence Pole Remover, the job takes about a week and a half, according to Zaleski.The improvement cuts the schedule by roughly half. That allows the crew to complete the seasonal task sooner and return to other highway responsibilities.The device also reduces the physical stress placed on workers. Zaleski said that no one was getting hurt anymore during the operation and that the department could complete the job twice as fast.This combination of safety and efficiency is important. A tool that merely speeds up a dangerous task would not solve the underlying problem. Riverhead’s invention changes the method itself, making the work less dependent on repeated heavy pulling.Workers still need to use the device carefully, but the central strain has been shifted from the human body to the steel frame and wheel.How the remover worksThe design is based on a straightforward sequence.A worker positions the device beside a snow-fence pole and slides the box tubing over it. The tubing holds the pole while the operator moves the frame and applies force through the wheel.The wheel acts as a pivot or rolling support. As pressure is applied, the frame creates leverage that loosens the pole and lifts it from the frozen ground.The tool can then be moved to the next pole. Because it is light enough to manoeuvre and does not depend on a fuel-powered engine, workers can use it repeatedly across the fence line.Its simplicity also makes maintenance easier. If a component becomes damaged, the department can likely repair or replace it using ordinary workshop materials.That matters in highway operations, where equipment may be used in cold, wet and muddy conditions. A complicated machine can be effective, but it may also require specialised parts or service. Riverhead’s tool is built around components that are easy to understand and adapt.Recognition in New YorkThe Snow Fence Pole Remover first gained attention through New York’s statewide Build a Better Mousetrap Competition.The competition is organised by the New York State Local Technical Assistance Program Center’s Cornell Local Roads Program. It invites transportation agencies to submit tools, equipment modifications and processes designed or built by local workers.The programme looks for ideas that improve safety, reduce costs, increase efficiency or improve the quality of transportation work. It does not require every entry to be a physical gadget. A new maintenance process, technology application or public-management strategy can also qualify.Riverhead’s invention won first place in the statewide competition. That victory automatically moved it forward to the national Federal Highway Administration competition.The state competition gave the department a platform to show how a small local improvement could produce measurable results. The invention did not require a large budget or a major research team. Its strength came from solving a specific problem faced by the crew.The federal Pioneer AwardThe Federal Highway Administration selected Riverhead’s Snow Fence Pole Remover for the 2026 Pioneer Award.FHWA says the Pioneer Award went to the Town of Riverhead Highway Department for developing a cost-effective innovation made entirely from repurposed materials. The agency highlighted the tool’s ability to reduce physical strain while increasing productivity and safety.The award formed part of the 2026 Build a Better Mousetrap national competition. FHWA evaluated more than 100 combined submissions from 2025 and 2026, making the recognition especially notable for a small town highway department.Other 2026 winners included a custom culvert steamer hook-lift body created by the Claremont Department of Public Works in New Hampshire, an AI-powered street right-of-way inventory developed by the City of Santa Maria in California and a roadway survey mobile rig designed by Johnson County, Iowa.Those projects used different technologies and addressed different transportation problems. Riverhead’s submission stood out for its low-cost construction and direct effect on worker safety.Why Build a Better Mousetrap mattersThe competition is designed to share practical ideas across the transportation sector.Local highway departments often face similar challenges, including snow removal, drainage maintenance, road inspections, equipment repairs and roadside safety. A solution developed in one community may be adapted by another.The New York programme encourages agencies to document their ideas, submit photographs and provide videos when possible. The national competition can then help bring those local solutions to a wider audience.That process is valuable because many useful improvements remain informal. A worker may create a bracket, attachment or method that makes a job easier, but the idea may never reach another department.Recognition gives the invention credibility and encourages other agencies to consider whether they can build their own versions.The Riverhead tool could be particularly easy to reproduce. A department with a welding area, scrap steel and a suitable wheel may be able to create a similar device after adapting the dimensions to its own poles and soil conditions.The value of worker-led innovationZaleski developed the device after observing the people who performed the work.He also enjoys welding outside his role as highway superintendent, giving him the skills to turn the idea into a working tool. His practical knowledge helped him create a frame that could withstand repeated use and provide the necessary leverage.This type of innovation often begins with close attention rather than a formal design process. Workers understand which movements cause pain, where equipment fails and which parts of a job consume the most time.Managers may know the overall schedule and budget, but employees often understand the physical details of a task better than anyone else. When they are encouraged to improve the process, small changes can produce significant results.Zaleski said the invention was created to make the department’s work safer and easier. He did not expect it to become a national award winner.That modest origin is part of the tool’s appeal. It was not designed for publicity. It was designed because workers needed a better way to do their job.A zero-dollar successThe Snow Fence Pole Remover also demonstrates how public agencies can innovate under financial constraints.Highway departments have to prioritise spending across many needs. Winter operations, pavement repairs, drainage work, traffic signs and vehicle maintenance can consume much of an annual budget.A new specialised machine may be useful but difficult to justify if the department can solve the problem with materials already in storage.Riverhead’s device converted an old golf-cart wheel and scrap box tubing into equipment that saves labour hours and reduces injury risk. The tool did not need a grant, purchase order or commercial contract.The financial saving extends beyond the construction cost. Completing the work sooner may reduce overtime, free staff for other assignments and lower the cost associated with workplace injuries.The idea also encourages departments to reconsider what they keep in their workshops. Materials that appear outdated or unsuitable may become valuable when combined with a new design.More than a clever gadgetAlthough the invention is physically small, its effects reach several parts of highway operations.The faster removal schedule improves productivity. The lower physical strain supports employee safety. The zero-dollar construction cost protects public funds. The simple design makes the tool easier to repair and reproduce.These benefits reinforce one another. A safer tool can reduce lost workdays, while a faster tool can reduce the number of hours workers spend exposed to cold weather and repetitive lifting.The device may also improve morale. Employees are more likely to feel valued when management responds to a difficult working condition with a practical solution.Zaleski said that management may steer the department, but the workforce consists of the people doing the difficult work. He compared the workers to the people rowing the boat.That message reflects the broader meaning of the award. Public infrastructure depends on workers whose contributions are often unseen. Recognising their inventions highlights the knowledge built through daily maintenance.A model for other departmentsRiverhead’s invention may inspire other highway departments to design their own tools.A similar remover would need to be evaluated for safe operation. Different snow-fence poles may vary in diameter, length and material. Soil conditions can also affect the amount of force required, especially after freezing weather.Departments would need to test the design, train employees and establish procedures for using it around traffic, uneven ground and other equipment.Even if another agency does not copy the device exactly, it could adapt the principle. Leverage, wheels and scrap materials can be combined in different ways to solve related lifting and pulling problems.The Build a Better Mousetrap programme encourages precisely this kind of exchange. Its purpose is not only to reward one winning invention but to show how local transportation agencies can improve operations from within.A practical idea with a lasting impactThe Snow Fence Pole Remover began as a response to a familiar problem. Workers were spending weeks pulling frozen poles by hand, and the strain was causing injuries.Mike Zaleski built a solution from an old golf-cart wheel and scrap box tubing. The tool cost nothing, cut the job from about three weeks to a week and a half, and reduced the physical effort required from the crew.The Federal Highway Administration’s Pioneer Award now gives the invention national visibility. FHWA evaluated more than 100 submissions before selecting Riverhead among the 2026 winners.For the highway department, however, the most important recognition remains practical. The tool makes a difficult seasonal job faster and safer.Its story shows that innovation does not always require advanced technology or a large budget. Sometimes it begins with one worker noticing a problem, asking whether there is an easier way and using the materials already at hand to build it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Is Ethiopia on the verge of another civil war as fighting erupts in Tigray?
articles.summary: Seven armed groups have joined forces against Abiy Ahmed’s government, bringing former enemies into the same alliance.
articles.body:
Intensified fighting between Ethiopia’s federal army and forces from the northern region of Tigray has raised fears that the peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war in 2022 could collapse.

The escalation came days after seven armed groups from across Ethiopia formed a new alliance which seeks to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, with each side of the conflict blaming the other for instigating the latest flare-up in violence.

The immediate fear for many in the country is a return to the war they have spent nearly four years trying to recover from. Here is what we know.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, began as an armed movement against Ethiopia’s military government in the 1970s. It later became the dominant force in the coalition that governed Ethiopia for nearly three decades.

That influence was contentious in a country with many ethnic groups, where Tigrayans account for only about 6 percent of Ethiopia’s population. When Abiy became prime minister in 2018, he created the Prosperity Party to replace the governing coalition, sharply reducing the TPLF’s influence at the centre of government.

Relations between Abiy’s government and the TPLF deteriorated until war broke out in November 2020. Federal troops, Eritrean forces and some fighters from the neighbouring Amhara region fought against Tigrayan forces. The conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people, displaced millions and left Tigray largely cut off from the outside world.

A peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 ended the full-scale war. But it did not settle some of the disputes that had helped fuel it.

One of the deepest disputes concerns western Tigray. Fighters from the neighbouring Amhara region, who fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army during the 2020-2022 war, took control of western Tigray. Hundreds of thousands of Tigrayans were driven from their homes, and Tigrayan leaders now want the territory returned and those displaced to be allowed to return to their homes.

Many in Amhara reject Tigray’s claim to the territory, however. They argue that western Tigray should not have been incorporated into Tigray when Ethiopia’s regional boundaries were redrawn in 1992, after the fall of the military government.

That dispute is ongoing, even though the TPLF and the Amhara Fano National Movement have now joined the same alliance against Abiy Ahmed’s government.

The federal government also says Tigrayan forces have retained weapons they were meant to surrender. Tigrayan leaders, in turn, say the government has failed to secure the withdrawal of other forces or enable displaced people to return home, particularly to western Tigray.

The political arrangements made after the war have also broken down. The TPLF faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael retook control of Tigray’s administration earlier this year, displacing an interim administration established under the peace agreement.

“Since the end of the war, while the Pretoria Agreement has held, there have been consistent violations on both sides,” Jervin Naidoo, a senior political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, told Al Jazeera. He said Tigrayans remained aggrieved over western Tigray, the presence of outside forces and the region’s autonomy.

The government sees the TPLF differently. Naidoo said it would portray the group as “a belligerent group trying to destabilise Ethiopia”. But for Tigrayan leaders, he said, renewed fighting could be presented as a matter of protecting their region.

The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival was announced this month by seven armed movements. Its largest members include the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). It also includes groups from Ethiopia’s Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz areas.

They have different aims and histories, but share a stated objective – to remove Abiy’s government.

Their agreement marks a striking reversal of the alliances formed during the last war, with Fano fighters who fought alongside federal troops against the TPLF now fighting alongside the TPLF.

The Pretoria agreement helped reshape those relationships. It ended the war between Addis Ababa and the TPLF, but Eritrea and Amhara forces, which had supported the government, were not parties to it. Both later fell out with Abiy’s government.

The alliance extends beyond northern Ethiopia. The OLA has fought federal forces in Oromia, in central Ethiopia, since 2018, while a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) has joined despite a separate peace agreement signed with the government that year. The ONLF leadership inside Ethiopia’s Somali region says it is not part of the new coalition.

Common opposition to Abiy does not mean the groups agree on Ethiopia’s future. Tigrayan and Amhara members still have competing claims to western Tigray. The government has also accused Eritrea of backing the alliance. Eritrea has repeatedly denied supporting the armed groups.

Small-scale clashes and reported drone strikes preceded this week’s escalation. Fighting then intensified in southern Tigray and spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.

Each side blames the other for starting the latest major clashes. Tigrayan forces say they responded to a federal offensive involving ground troops and drones. The government side accuses the TPLF of attacking first. With the fighting continuing, claims about individual attacks and territorial gains are difficult to verify independently.

“There has been overnight fighting in the border town of Abala,” Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi reported from Kenya. The town, located in northern Afar on the border with Tigray, was also affected by the previous war. Reports have differed over who controls the town. On a separate front in Amhara, Ethiopia’s army says it killed more than 270 rebel fighters. That figure has not been independently verified.

Tigrayan forces have taken control of the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire, disrupting civilian flights. The African Union says the seizure is inconsistent with the Pretoria agreement. About three-quarters of a million people remained displaced within Tigray because of the earlier war before this latest escalation.

There is a risk it could, but analysts say the conflict has not descended into a full-scale civil war yet. Fighting has crossed Tigray’s borders, and the federal government is already facing armed conflicts in other regions.

There is also a chance of regional escalation. Eritrea fought alongside the Ethiopian government during the previous Tigray war, but relations between the neighbours have since deteriorated, partly over Abiy’s push for access to Red Sea ports. Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia.

The African Union has called for an immediate halt to the escalation and for renewed talks under the Pretoria agreement. It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who helped mediate the 2022 deal, to engage the parties urgently. The East African bloc IGAD has also urged neighbouring countries to avoid actions that could make the crisis worse.

articles.title: Damaged fragment deemed 'unremarkable' turns out to be rare piece of Homer's 'Odyssey' history
articles.summary: A fragment of Homer's "Odyssey" Book 12 sat unnoticed for decades in Utrecht University's archives until a Radboud University professor recognized it.
articles.body: An ancient fragment of Homer's "Odyssey" was hiding in plain sight for decades in a university library in the Netherlands — until a professor took a closer look. The discovery, announced by Utrecht University this month, was made in the university's Special Collections. Mark de Kreij, an assistant professor of Ancient Greek and Papyrology at Radboud University, came across the unidentified parchment while studying Greek manuscripts in the university's collection. EXPERTS STUNNED AFTER UNCOVERING HOMER'S 'ILIAD' ON EGYPTIAN MUMMY IN UNPRECEDENTED FIND De Kreij told Fox News Digital the fragment had originally been kept with Coptic Christian manuscripts, which he said was "probably why it was missed in the early research on the collection." By the time he examined it, however, the still-unidentified fragment had been moved to a box containing Greek manuscripts. Utrecht University said the fragment was first considered ordinary. "Hidden among these, first regarded as an unremarkable 7th-century fragment, was a damaged and discolored fragment with very small, neat letters," the university said. "De Kreij soon recognized a few words typical of the Homeric epics." ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CITY HIDDEN BENEATH EGYPT'S DESERT The fragment contains verses from Book 12 of the "Odyssey" — including the pivotal moment when the sun god Helios discovers that Odysseus' crew killed and ate his sacred cattle. Helios then demands vengeance from Zeus — an episode recently depicted in the Christopher Nolan film adaptation. Researchers believe the manuscript was owned by a reader living in Egypt's Fayum oasis, southwest of modern-day Cairo, around 300 A.D. The fragment has been dated to the 3rd or 4th century A.D. And its age isn't the only thing that makes it a rarity. The university says only a few fragments like it exist across the world. ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS BATTLES COULD BE REWRITTEN BY LONG-LOST PAPAL LETTER "There are only around 30 fragments like it worldwide," the statement said. Though the university described the fragment as part of a "pocket edition" of the complete epic, one expert told Fox News Digital she was not convinced by that interpretation. "This is something that people held in their hand. This is something they carried with them." Anna Dolganov, a Roman historian and papyrologist at the Austrian Archaeological Institute of the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna, questioned whether the fragment came from a complete copy of Homer's epic. "The entire ‘Odyssey’ would require 480 pages," she said. ANCIENT BOOK OF REVELATION CITY GIVES UP STUNNING SECRET BURIED FOR 1,500 YEARS Dolganov noted that a parchment volume of that length would be extremely thick in such a small format — making it unlikely, in her view, that the codex contained the entire epic. The expert also pointed to the handwriting, which she described as more casual and cursive than what she would expect in a complete literary work. "What I think it's more likely to be is an anthology," she posited. "Or a private collection of excerpts from literary texts, possibly for use in schools, for education, or a private anthology that would have been much, much smaller — not the entire 'Odyssey.'" De Kreij pointed to the text preserved on both sides of the parchment as evidence that it belonged to a complete copy of the epic. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Both sides contain passages from book 12 of the ‘Odyssey,’ which are nearly contiguous," he told Fox News Digital. De Kreij said an anthology is theoretically possible, but he knows of no similar examples from the period. Complete copies of works such as the "Iliad" and "Odyssey," by contrast, have numerous parallels, he said. Dolganov said the discovery also reflects Homer's widespread popularity in the ancient world, where his works played an important role in education. The ancient poet "was very popular indeed all over the Mediterranean world where Greek was learned," Dolganov said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Homer was used to teach Greek," she added, explaining that his works were widely used as school texts around the Eastern Mediterranean. Dolganov noted that dating ancient literary manuscripts can be difficult and imprecise, particularly in situations where scholars rely on handwriting as evidence. "It would be important not to overstate how certain we are that this is indeed as early as the third or fourth century," she said. "But it doesn't need to be, to be a very interesting and exciting discovery," she said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ De Kreij said the dating is based on several features of the fragment, including its codex format, parchment material, the appearance of the ink and its handwriting. "The neat, small bookhand cannot be dated with absolute certainty, but there are good parallels from the late third and fourth century," he said. "All such dating has to be approximate, but in the scientific edition, I cite a number of dated parallels to back up my estimate." "This is something they carried with them and read, and it's a text that's also accessible to us." "So it kind of connects us to the ancient reader because we are similarly excited by this timeless work of literature."

articles.title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
articles.summary: The UK's busiest airport cautions it may miss the government target of 2035 as ministers say the deadline has "always been ambitious".
articles.body:
Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.

The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost £33bn, would open by 2035.

But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".

The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.

The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission.

It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace".

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025 as a means to grow the economy, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office.

Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy as part of a wider £49bn modernisation of the airport.

The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway.

The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan has always opposed the new runway, warning of the impact on noise, air pollution and climate change.

The government's climate advisers warned last week that the expansion should only go ahead if airlines were required to pay for cleaner flying, which could push up the cost of flights.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the advisers had set out "one view" but there was "more than one pathway to meeting our climate change obligations", in an interview with the Daily Telegraph published on Friday.

A draft of the planning framework for the expansion was published in June this year for consultation. Once finalised, it then needs to be put to a parliamentary vote, which could reportedly be delayed until 2027.

What's the plan for a third runway at Heathrow Airport?

Third Heathrow runway should only go ahead if airlines pay for cleaner flying, say advisers

Heathrow expansion an 'outdated' risk, mayor says

A DfT spokesperson said: "There is currently no live planning application for a third runway, and we cannot comment on ongoing consultation processes or prejudice them in a way that will only delay progress.

"The timeline has always been ambitious. We'll continue to work with promoters, including Heathrow, and all other stakeholders at pace to ensure the right framework is in place for which a planning application for a third runway could be considered."

A spokesperson for Heathrow said: "It's right that ambitious targets were set; the sooner expansion begins, the sooner the whole UK will benefit."

They said the benefits would involve "at least 108,000 new jobs and billions of pounds invested in supply chains in every part of the country".

"This is a national project, 100% privately financed which will support growth today and secure the UK's position in the global economy once the runway opens."

Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways.

articles.body: A Missouri substitute teacher says she lost her job after the staffing company that placed her in schools discovered that she had been running an OnlyFans account for more than two years.Sheena Sittner, who worked as a substitute teacher in the St Louis County area, said she had continued teaching while maintaining the account and knew there was always a possibility that her online activity could eventually be discovered.“I've had this account, this OnlyFans account, for two-plus years,” Sittner said, according to KTVI. She added that whoever discovered it must have gone looking for it because the account had existed for years.Sittner said she was surprised not only by the employment consequences but also by an instruction from Kelly Education, the company that hired her, telling her not to contact any school or school district.According to emails shared by Sittner, she was suspended pending termination and was told: “Please refrain from contacting any school or districts.”The warning became particularly significant for Sittner because her child attends a school in the district. She said she could deal with losing her job and facing criticism, but objected to the possibility of being prevented from participating in her child's education.“My personal life is completely separate from my professional life. I have kept those two separate forever,” Sittner said.School district clarifies teacher can remain involved as parentThe school district later clarified that Sittner could participate in her child's school life like any other parent.A district spokesman said she had passed a background check and completed the required online safety training and therefore could volunteer and participate in school activities.Kelly Education also clarified that its instruction applied only to Sittner's professional role. The company said it did not and could not restrict her rights as a parent or prevent her from participating in her child's education.Sittner said she had turned to adult content creation partly because of financial pressures and argued that better teacher pay could reduce the need for educators to seek additional sources of income.“If teachers were paid better, women wouldn't have to resort to online content creation,” she said. “Sex sells.”Missouri has seen similar OnlyFans controversiesSittner's case comes after other Missouri educators faced employment consequences after their OnlyFans activities became public.In 2023, St Clair High School English teacher Brianna Coppage resigned after administrators discovered her OnlyFans account. Coppage had said she was earning about $42,000 as a teacher and had started creating adult content to supplement her income.The issue later followed Coppage into another job. The company said she had violated its social-media policy, although Coppage said she was not given a detailed explanation of how she had violated the policy.Missouri's Department of Elementary and Secondary Education says substitute teachers must meet state certification requirements, including background clearance for new certificates or new hires. articles.title: Florida real estate sees surge from Washington high earners fleeing new millionaire income tax
articles.summary: Pacific Northwest millionaires are buying Florida real estate as Washington state's looming 9.9% income tax hike pushes high-net-worth individuals south.
articles.body: Washington state millionaires are increasingly eyeing Florida real estate to escape a changing tax landscape in the Pacific Northwest, according to a luxury real estate expert. "I would say that the first thing is taxes. Income tax in Florida is 0%, and in Washington state, it's 9.9% as of January 2028," Margit Brandt, a luxury property specialist, told Fox News Digital. "Capital gains in Florida is also 0%, and in Washington state, it's 7%. I just think that they've created this really punitive tax environment that's unappealing to the high-net-worth individuals who are the high earners in Washington State, and that's been the biggest kind of feeder for our market here," she added. Washington's capital gains tax is tiered, with the first $1 million in taxable Washington capital gains subject to a 7% rate and amounts above $1 million subject to a 9.9% rate. Real estate is exempt from the tax. TRUCKING COMPANY OWNER SUING STATE OVER 'MILLIONAIRES TAX' SAYS POLICY HITS SMALL BUSINESSES The push comes after the Democratic-controlled Washington Legislature passed, and Gov. Bob Ferguson signed, a 9.9% levy on annual adjusted gross income above the law's $1 million threshold. Set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2028 — with initial returns due in April 2029 — the legislation marks a major change for a state that currently has no individual income tax. The tax is already facing a court challenge over its constitutionality, while real estate insiders say the new law is influencing some wealthy residents' relocation decisions. SEATTLE MAYOR SHRUGS OFF MILLIONAIRE-TAX CONCERNS AS 44% OF BUSINESS LEADERS CONSIDER LEAVING "We've seen actual deals — big deals — happen with high earners from Washington state," Brandt said. "This is not hypothetical. These are closed transactions with people setting up a whole new life here in Florida." While comprehensive data tracking millionaire migration following the new tax are not yet available, a recent business survey found increased interest among respondents in relocating. A recent survey released by the Association of Washington Business (AWB) — the state's chamber of commerce and manufacturers association — found that 24% of respondents said they were considering moving their businesses out of Washington. That figure is up from 17% in the previous quarter and nearly triple the rate recorded 16 months ago. Furthermore, 55% of surveyed business leaders said they are considering moving their personal residence to another state — a number that climbs to 67% in Spokane County, near the low-tax Idaho border. WHY STARBUCKS PICKED NASHVILLE OVER SEATTLE FOR EXPANSION, ACCORDING TO LOCAL BUSINESS REPORTER The shift is mirrored in high-profile individual departures. Jesse Proudman, founder and CTO of privacy-focused AI platform Venice.ai, told Fox News Digital in May that he was leaving the Evergreen State, warning that a region once known as a "startup sanctuary" has grown increasingly hostile to business leaders. Similarly, coffee giant Starbucks announced in April that it would invest $100 million to set up an additional support office in Nashville, Tennessee — a state with no individual income tax — where it expects to have 2,000 support jobs over the next five years. Starbucks said those jobs will include newly created positions, work brought in-house and some teams moved from Seattle. Beyond balance sheets, Brandt said that safety, culture, and quality of life are primary drivers for wealthy transplants moving to Florida and other states, including Texas and the Carolinas. It's a whole new lifestyle," Brandt said, adding that Florida’s lack of a state estate tax and its proximity to the Caribbean appeal heavily to multi-generational wealth. "They want safety, security, good schools, and to set up their financial future. Florida is just such an easy landing place, and I think we're going to see way more of it in the coming years." articles.body: Oxford, Mississippi, Mayor Robyn Tannehill issued a stark warning Saturday about the dangers of kratom and other "gas station drugs" after packaged kratom was recovered during investigations into the deaths of two Ole Miss students.
