articles.title: One year on, the UK’s recognition of Palestinian statehood is bearing fruit
articles.summary: The British government is moving to translate rhetoric into policy.
articles.body:
This week marks one year since the United Kingdom, along with nine other Western countries , recognised the State of Palestine. What shifted was politics, not policy: overwhelming support for the Palestinian cause by the British public finally persuaded the government to align with the law.

For decades, the UK backed a two-state solution in words only. Its logic was twisted: recognise statehood only after a final peace agreement, handing Israel a veto over the very policy it claimed to support, even as successive Israeli governments worked – through words, bulldozers and bombs – to render Palestinian statehood impossible.

This approach treated Palestinian self-determination as conditional, not an inalienable right — earned through reform, “good governance” and benchmarks no other people have been made to meet.

The British recognition of Palestinian statehood marked a turning point – one that is already bearing fruit a year later. Upgrading relations with Palestine has allowed the UK to turn rhetoric into policy.

Almost a year after the UK formally recognised the State of Palestine, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that the British government now regards the Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands as unlawful.

He then set out bans on settlement goods, services, advertising and arms licences, as well as sanctions on companies that build, finance or sell settlement homes. This move is a logical next step after the British recognition of Palestinian statehood.

The British foreign secretary, to his credit, acknowledged Britain should have acted sooner. Prime Minister Andy Burnham put it plainly: support for two states is “meaningless unless we back it up with action”.

The legal groundwork for these measures was laid in July 2024, when the International Court of Justice declared Israel’s occupation unlawful, along with the separation wall and settlements, and its near-total separation of settlers to be equivalent to racial segregation and apartheid. The court ruled the occupation must end “as rapidly as possible”.

After Miliband’s announcement, 11 other governments, including Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, ⁠Poland, Portugal, Spain, and ⁠Sweden, joined a parallel statement on sanctions and trade with settlements.

These measures matter because the occupation runs on an ecosystem of contractors, lenders, estate agents and Israeli state institutions sponsoring the settlements — and the new rules must reach every part of it. For decades, words on Palestine cost nothing while settlements multiplied; now there are consequences.

Israel has responded. It has ordered London to close its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which it cannot legally do since it holds no sovereignty there. The punitive measures unleashed onto the Palestinian population are worse still.

Since September 2, Israeli forces have demolished every home in Khirbet al-Tabban and northern al-Fakhit in the occupied West Bank, leaving roughly 70 people, 28 of them children, without shelter.

Settlement activities have also accelerated. Earlier this month, the occupation authorities issued tenders for 3,401 planned housing units as part of the E1 project, which would cut off occupied East Jerusalem from the occupied West Bank.

In Gaza, where two million of our people are confined to less than 30 percent of the Strip’s territory, Israel continues to bomb and kill civilians. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called ceasefire began last October last year. Meanwhile, more than 140,000 tarpaulins and 7,500 tents meant to provide shelter for the winter for homeless Palestinians sit blocked in the Jordan corridor.

For too long, countries like the UK exercised caution and hesitation, sending the wrong signal to Israel, inviting more aggressive action and solidifying its culture of impunity.

For that to change, the announced sanction measures need to be followed by action.

First, there needs to be immediate and full implementation. The sanctions must be put into practice and the 12 governments should agree on how they will respond to pressure to reverse course. Unity can help withstand coercion.

Second, there needs to be protection for the people these measures exist for. The olive harvest begins next month in Palestine. During last year’s harvest, the United Nations recorded 126 settler attacks in 70 towns and villages within its first three weeks. This year’s harvest is the first real test of whether settler sanctions carry weight on the ground.

Collective action should not be limited to the occupied West Bank. There must be efforts to end the ongoing genocide in Gaza and Israel’s continuing violations of the ceasefire. Urgently, there needs to be pressure to secure the delivery of aid, particularly the much-needed shelter materials held in the Jordan corridor.

Moving forward, we must remember the example of apartheid South Africa. The boycott and sanctions campaign was resisted by Western governments, including the British one, and their action is remembered now as lagging behind their people.

This time, the UK can lead and be judged differently, if it holds its nerve, moving together with a growing number of partners, as it did with the 11 other governments two weeks ago.

Next year marks 110 years since the Balfour Declaration, 80 since the UN partition vote, and 60 since the occupation began. Palestine has had enough beginnings. What it needs now is an ending.

For the first time in a generation, law, politics and sentiment in London are beginning to point the same way. This is Britain’s chance to lead a better future and redeem the past.

When the occupation ends, and it will, the path to a peace rooted in justice, dignity and equality can finally be laid.

articles.title: German town bans stumbling stone memorials to Nazi victims
articles.summary: Germany's education minister has branded the ban on the small brass memorial plaques a "scandal".
articles.body:
There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis.

Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal".

Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria, have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities.

The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations.

But now councillors from the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones - or "Stolpersteine" in German - in their town.

The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects.

The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate.

Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated.

However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision.

"Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild.

She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision.

Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach".

She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD".

Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance – which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance.

In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings.

As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location.

Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen".

The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects.

Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

articles.title: 'No turning back' in independence journey, says Wales' first minister
articles.summary: It is the first time the first minister of Wales has attended a Yes Cymru march.
articles.body:
Wales' first minister has said there is "no turning back" on the journey to indepence for the country, as he attended a rally on Saturday.

In a speech addressing the crowd gathered in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, Rhun ap Iorwerth said the "next step" for Wales had to be "equality with Scotland, as a minimum".

Thousands were in attendance, with the event organisers, campaign group Yes Cymru, saying it estimated the march attracted between 8,000 and 9,000 people.

"[Wales is] on a journey, and there's no turning back," ap Iorwerth said.

Since 2019, thousands have taken part in independence marches across Wales, including in Cardiff, Swansea, Wrexham, Merthyr Tydfil, Rhyl and Barry.

But this was the first time the first minister of Wales had attended a Yes Cymru march.

A Reform Cymru Member of the Senedd (MS) said he was "disappointed" by the first minister's decision to attend, while a Welsh Conservative MS said it would be "better for him to be behind his desk in Cathays sorting the problems he said he would sort out".

Following the march, a rally in Castle Gardens featured speeches, including from the fiest minister, as well as Yes Cymru's chairman Rob Hughes and Elwyn Vaughan, Plaid Cymru MS for Gwynedd Maldwyn.

It was the first march since the pro-independence party Plaid Cymru came into government in Wales following the Senedd elections in May.

Ap Iorwerth said: "We are standing up for Wales, pursuing the investment and greater powers we need from Westminster now, so we can make a real difference to people's lives as the next step in our constitutional journey."

In his speech, the Plaid Cymru MS for Bangor Conwy Môn referenced Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments yesterday, ruling out the handing of powers to hold a referendum on independence to the Welsh government.

"The right to self-determination is not a right that the UK government is willing to acknowledge," ap Iorwerth said.

This week, the Senedd narrowly rejected a Reform motion declaring Wales should remain part of the United Kingdom.

The vote was initially tied, with 45 members backing the motion and 45 opposed, requiring Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies to cast the deciding vote against the proposal in line with parliamentary convention.

Reform MS Joe Martin said the first minister's attendance at the event was "disappointing to see, especially so early in the term, given that Plaid Cymru campaigned on a platform where independence wasn't on the table for the Senedd term".

"It's not where their priorities and their attention should be," he told Politics Wales .

"If there was a clear and overwhelming majority of people in Wales who wanted independence then obviously that would change things, but there isn't, there's a clear and overwhelming majority of people who don't want independence."

Andrew RT Davies MS from the Welsh Conservatives added that "waiting times have gone up, and we've had the Pisa results that shows we've fallen further behind other parts of the United Kingdom. So instead of marching in Aberystwyth, [the first minister would] better off behind his desk in Cathays sorting the problems that he said he would sort out".

Responding to the opposition parties' criticism, a spokesperson for Plaid Cymru said: "We are getting on with the priorities facing Wales right now - reducing NHS waiting times, improving literacy and numeracy, supporting jobs and businesses, and tackling the cost of living - while also standing up for Wales and being ambitious for our nation's future."

articles.title: Blue plaque unveiled in honour of Mott the Hoople singer in Oswestry
articles.summary: Ian Hunter says the plaque at his birth place is an honour and he is a "Shropshire lad at heart".
articles.body:
A blue plaque has been installed at the house where Mott the Hoople lead singer Ian Hunter was born in Oswestry.

The plaque was unveiled on York Street on Saturday by the town's mayor, councillor Jonathan Upton, and Hunter's eldest grandson, Jay Patterson.

In a video message shared by the town council, Hunter, who now lives in Connecticut in the US and was unable to attend the unveiling in person, thanked the organisers and said it was a "surprise and an honour".

"I'm still a Shropshire lad at heart," he told fans. "I'm eternally grateful for your love and your support - it's been 50 odd years, when you're 87, you do need a little support."

The plaque installation had been organised by councillor Duncan Kerr after permission was granted by Oswestry Town Council.

Formed in Herefordshire in the 1960s, Mott the Hoople's best-remembered single is 1972 hit All The Young Dudes, written by David Bowie.

The band split in 1974, but have reformed on a number of occasions for tours and live gigs.

Patterson, who himself is also a musician, said he was surprised by the number of people who turned out to attend the unveiling.

The round plaque, which features a lyric from Hunter's 1976 track Irene Wilde, "gonna be somebody someday", meant a "huge amount" to the family, he said.

"Growing up, we always knew who my granddad was, he was just pops to all of us. But then, obviously, when you have days like today, it really does just go to show how much of a legend he was and how much he's loved by his fans," Patterson explained.

"To have something commemorate not just his career, but his life and where he was born, it's a massive thing for us as a family."

Kerr, who is also a Mott the Hoople fan, said he was passionate about smaller towns celebrating "legends" who were born there.

"I just think it's powerful to walk past a plaque on a wall and say, ‘here's somebody who almost conquered the world, certainly conquered America, who was born on your street’," the green councillor added.

"I think the town benefits from that, tourism benefits from that, but I think young people benefit from that as well."

Some fans had travelled to the event from as far as Kent, Swansea and Stoke-on-Trent, Kerr said.

"[Hunter] meant a lot to them. He touched a lot of people's lives and they wanted to come and pay their respects back to him and it's lovely to do that when he's still alive," he added.

One fan, Sean Stewart, who travelled from Nantwich, added Hunter had been part of his musical life since he was about six or seven years old.

"Ever since then I've just always had Ian Hunter's music in my bones. It's just always worked for me."

Graham Jones, who travelled from Lichfield, said it was Hunter's musicianship and lyrics that had appealed to him most.

"I think the overall quality of his own musicianship and the quality of the musicians he surrounded himself with, but it was the lyrical content really that got me in the first place," he said.

articles.title: Several hundred thousand people gather for Pope Leo’s mass in Paris
articles.summary: Vatican estimates 700,000 people in attendance as the Catholic religious leader continues four-day tour of France.
articles.body:
Several hundred thousand people have gathered in the French capital to attend Pope Leo XIV’s outdoor mass.

The Vatican estimated that 700,000 people came out in Paris on Saturday, more than the 600,000 who had registered in advance.

The American pope greeted flag-waving, cheering throngs from his popemobile as he rode along France’s 1.9 kilometres (1.2 miles) famous avenue, the Champs-Elysees.

Upon arriving at Place de la Concorde, Paris’s largest public square, Leo held an outdoor mass and led hundreds of thousands of people in prayer.

The pontiff began his four-day tour of France on Friday , marking the first official papal visit to the country in 18 years.

The pope is seeking to improve the Roman Catholic Church’s standing in France, five years after an inquiry found that 330,000 children were abused by its clergy and lay members over the span of seven decades. The religious leader has also been challenging France’s recently approved law allowing assisted dying.

French President Emmanuel Macron was not present for the mass and was represented by his wife, Brigitte. Far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen was also among the attendees. Le Pen currently leads the polls in advance of next year’s election, which is due to take place in mid-April.

The pope is next due to travel to the southwestern town of Lourdes, where he will meet seven French victims abused by members of the clergy on Sunday.

On Friday, an estimated 300,000 people turned out to see the pontiff as he waved from the popemobile on the way to the Notre Dame Cathedral.

“There is a sense of fervour reminiscent of that experienced over 40 years ago with John Paul II,” Francois Mabille, director of the Geopolitical Observatory on Religion, told broadcaster RMC.

The pontiff met Macron on Friday and gave a rare speech at his official residence, the Elysee Palace.

He praised French society, describing it as the result of “a people whose diverse origins have enlivened and enriched the nation and its democracy”.

He also spoke out against AI , warning that “a paradise of machines” could cause people to lose their humanity.

The Catholic Church has gradually seen its influence in secular France dwindle in recent decades.

articles.title: Ohio college janitor hid in ceiling above locker room to photograph women’s soccer team, police say
articles.summary: A janitor at Wilmington College in Ohio was arrested Tuesday for hiding in the ceiling above a locker room to photograph the women’s soccer team as they changed, police said.
articles.body: A janitor at Wilmington College in Ohio was arrested Tuesday for hiding in the ceiling above a locker room to photograph the women’s soccer team as they changed, police said. Jayson Barker was charged with 11 counts of voyeurism after a member of the team spotted the alleged offender snapping photos from above in a locker room at the Scheve Athletic Center. Barker was detained by campus security until police arrived. He was held on $22,000 bail at a nearby jail after his arrest but has since been released after posting it, according to the police and jail officials. Wilmington College said in a statement that Barker worked for a vendor and that the school’s relationship with the custodial services contractor has since been terminated. “The College’s paramount concern is the safety and well-being of its students,” Wilmington College said in a statement. “We have been providing counseling and other support services for the affected students since Tuesday night and are taking measures to ensure that no student’s safety or well-being is compromised.” Investigators are trying to determine whether Barker has a history of similar conduct. He could face additional charges. Barker is next due in court on Oct. 5.

articles.title: CJI says drug abuse among children a protection crisis, seeks rehabilitation
articles.summary: CJI Surya Kant calls child drug abuse a protection crisis, urges rehab with counselling, education, safe care, and strict action against traffickers.
articles.body: Patna: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Saturday called for a shift in the way society responds to children caught in substance abuse, saying the problem must be viewed as a child protection crisis, not merely an issue of health or crime.Addressing a lecture on “Childhood beyond drugs: Protection, care and reintegration” at Lok Bhavan under the Patliputra Pragya Pravah series, the CJI said, “When a child encounters intoxicating substances, education gets interrupted, family relationships may become strained and physical and mental health suffer.” Children caught in addiction, he warned, become vulnerable to exploitation, violence, trafficking and illegal activities.“Substance abuse among children must therefore be understood not only as a public health concern, but equally as a child protection concern,” he said.Surya Kant said peer pressure, neglect, violence, poverty and troubled home environments could push children towards drugs. “The child must be helped, not condemned.”He said freeing a child from drugs was only the beginning. Treatment must go hand in hand with counselling, mental-health support, education and a safe environment. Children should not be returned to unsafe homes and alternative care must be provided where necessary.He also called for stringent action against those who draw children into drug trafficking and exploit their vulnerability. “Any child’s past trouble should not become the identity of his or her future,” he said, stressing the need to replace stigma with dignity, support and a second chance.Governor Syed Ata Hasnain said the drug problem among children could not be reduced to crime or healthcare, pointing to its impact on education, family, security and their future. He stressed the need to monitor trafficking networks and said a child caught in drugs was not always an offender but could itself be a victim.Both stressed coordinated action by the judiciary, govt, police, health and education departments, child-protection institutions and civil society for rehabilitation and reintegration.The programme was attended by Patna high court Chief Justice Justice V Kameshwar Rao, Justice Sudhir Singh, chief secretary Pratyaya Amrit, advocate general S D Sanjay, additional chief secretary to the governor Deepak Kumar Singh and other administrative, police and judicial officials.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news. articles.title: ‘If I cut my hair, it’s an issue’: Chennai mayor Priya speaks out against cyber bullying
articles.summary: CHENNAI: Chennai mayor R Priya on Saturday spoke out against online trolling and cyberbullying targeting her, saying almost everything she does has been
articles.body: CHENNAI: Chennai mayor R Priya on Saturday spoke out against online trolling and cyberbullying targeting her, saying almost everything she does has been twisted into a controversy. “If I eat a burger, it’s an issue. If I cut my hair, it’s an issue. Every personal choice I make seems to be questioned and judged,” she said.“Sometimes I wonder if it is because I am a woman, or because I belong to a particular community? When it comes to me, I have no idea where the feminists and those who claim to stand up for women disappear,” she said.Her remarks came a day after she was trolled online apparently because of her new hairstyle during Friday’s Greater Chennai Corporation council meeting. Priya said from day one, even the simplest things she had done became an issue.Priya said women in politics were not “characterless or any less deserving of respect” and that being a woman in public life did not give anyone the right to judge her based on her appearance, lifestyle or personal choices. “Every woman has her own dignity, self-respect, and right to live her life on her own terms. Beyond the position of mayor, please remember to respect the woman,” she said.DMK MP Kanimozhi backed Priya, saying every choice made by women in public life should not be met with constant scrutiny and mockery.“Breaking into politics in a patriarchal society is tough enough; doing so from an oppressed community is even harder. Targeting women who push through these barriers is completely unacceptable. I strongly condemn these relentless, orchestrated controversies against the mayor,” Kanimozhi said in an X post.She questioned chief minister C Joseph Vijay over why he was allowing his fans and cadre to target Priya.Last month, Priya had lodged a complaint with the Chennai city commissioner of police against online trolling and cyberbullying. articles.title: Three held for bomb attacks on two houses
articles.summary: Kerala police arrested three suspects in Chirayinkeezhu for hurling crude bombs at two homes in Puthukari, allegedly linked to a property dispute.
articles.body: T’puram: Chirayinkeezhu Police arrested three persons in connection with the alleged hurling of crude bombs at two houses in Puthukari and nearby areas within a fortnight.The arrested are Ranjith and Ajeesh, both of Menamkulam, and Vaishnav of Keezhattingal. The police said they were arrested at Vangalamukku, where they had allegedly been staying after the attacks.According to the police, the accused were allegedly hired to carry out the attacks in connection with a property dispute. Further probe is under way.Recently, Puthukari Vayal native Vijayan’s house was attacked by the accused. Four crude bombs were allegedly hurled at the house while nine members of the family were inside. Three bombs exploded, and the fourth was later recovered and defused. articles.title: Nandini Milk price hike on hold; Karnataka chief minister seeks data from other states
articles.summary: Nandini milk price hike in Karnataka put on hold as CM DK Shivakumar seeks data from neighbouring states; cabinet to decide after reports from unions.
articles.body: Bengaluru: A demand for a steep hike in milk prices will now go before the state cabinet, possibly next week, with chief minister DK Shivakumar putting off an immediate decision even as thousands of farmers gathered in the city to press for relief.Representatives of milk unions met CM Saturday, seeking a hike of Rs 8-10 per litre for Nandini milk, of which Rs 2 could go directly to producers’ cooperatives. About 50,000 milk producers had assembled in Bengaluru demanding the increase.“We will examine it in the cabinet. I’m also getting reports on the situation in neighbouring states such as Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh,” Shivakumar said after meeting the unions.Shivakumar’s brother and Bangalore Milk Union Ltd (BAMUL) president DK Suresh said dairy farmers were under severe financial strain, with unions telling Karnataka Milk Federation that costs of cattle feed, veterinary care and transport had all risen sharply.Farmers argued a hike was overdue, pointing out that cooperatives in states such as Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh were already paying higher rates per litre, a gap that risked pushing local milk supply towards these neighbouring markets.Rather than approving an immediate increase, CM has asked officials and union functionaries to submit detailed reports comparing cattle feed price trends over the past decade and the rates paid in other states.
